channel.title: Francisco Roa — Posts
channel.description: Platform engineering from practice: Terraform at scale, multi-tenant Kubernetes, AI platforms and agent workflows.

item.title: A marketplace of one — versioning your own AI skills
item.description: Assistant skills drift and fork like dotfiles. Moving every skill, agent and hook into a local plugin marketplace — versioned plugins, symlinked single source, installed per session — makes every future session consistent.

item.title: Disaster recovery is a rehearsal, not a binder
item.description: Region loss as a scheduled event: critical data already lives in a second geography, one region pair is the designated restore target, and a weekly pipeline rehearses the restore into an isolated resource group and asserts the data is usable.

item.title: A backup is a tag, not a ticket
item.description: One tag — data_criticality — routes every resource to the right vault pair: GeoZone-redundant with paired-region restore for critical, Zone-redundant for important. DINE policies and daily discovery enforce enrolment; nobody files a backup ticket.

item.title: A raw model key is a budget with no owner and no off switch
item.description: Model keys never leave the platform: every AI call goes through a GenAI gateway — per-app subscription keys, hard token budgets, per-app×model metering, managed identity to the backend. Clients change one line: base_url.

item.title: Blender now takes a chat message as input, and that changes who can 3D-model
item.description: blender-mcp wires an MCP server into Blender so an assistant can drive the modeling tool directly from plain language. The interesting part isn't the demo — it's who gets to touch 3D work now.

item.title: "What happens when it dies?" is the whole architecture review
item.description: Delete a box from the diagram and read what's left. Ask it of the hub, the ONE gateway, a whole region — the answer is either a design property (a PDB, a cell boundary, run-once placement) or a war story. War stories are findings.

item.title: One gateway, one login: SSO for every tenant route
item.description: Move the OAuth dance out of the apps: one shared Traefik gateway, and an oauth2-proxy that fronts each tenant app — as forwardAuth middleware, or as this platform's default: a sidecar with per-tenant client, cookie and blast radius.

item.title: The sidecar pattern: capabilities a pod wears, not code it imports
item.description: Sidecar, ambassador, adapter — where this platform uses each (oauth2-proxy, Dapr, OTel), what a sidecar really costs, and the rule for when a DaemonSet beats N sidecars.

item.title: The cheapest cost review happens before the merge
item.description: A billing review three weeks after the merge is archaeology. Price the Terraform plan in the MR (Infracost), meter reality in the cluster (OpenCost), and gate like the safety gate — feedback loop first, hard block only for the GPU-sized risks.

item.title: Cost governance is three verbs: estimate, meter, standardize
item.description: Not a dashboard — a cycle: estimate at plan time, meter at runtime, standardize the metric so every cloud reports cost in the same shape. Plus the honest caveats: labels are the weakest link, and the integration needs an owner or it rots.

item.title: Golden paths fail when they're built for the platform team
item.description: The predictable failure modes — too many choices, one template for every workload, abandonment, no escape hatches — and the two metrics that matter: retention and bypass rate. Run the path as a product, not a launch.

item.title: An internal DevOps assistant is mostly plumbing, and MCP is the pipe
item.description: The useful assistant is an LLM with standardized read-only taps into git, metrics, cluster state and runbooks — evidence over eloquence, RBAC inherited, every request audited. MCP just makes the plumbing boring.

item.title: A good plan names the files before it touches them
item.description: A plan is the cheapest place to be wrong. Write it so a reviewer can kill the mistake before any code exists — name the exact files and edits, put the verification in the plan, and spend most of your words on what you will not do.

item.title: The cheapest bug to kill is still in the plan
item.description: Reviewing a plan beats reviewing the diff: a wrong assumption costs a sentence here and a rewrite there. Review the approach, the blast radius, the missing states and the escape hatch — then approve narrowly.

item.title: A skill is a prompt you only write once
item.description: A skill is the paved road for an agent — encode your conventions once instead of re-explaining them every session. One job, a description written to trigger it, the whole ceremony, and guardrails that bite.

item.title: Review a skill by the mistakes it prevents
item.description: You do not lint a skill, you taste-test it: does the description make it trigger at the right moment, do the steps survive a literal agent, and do the guardrails actually stop the failure you fear?

item.title: DNS is the platform's phone book — and its weakest excuse for an outage
item.description: Names as infrastructure: private zones so services resolve over the inspected path, records generated from live ingresses, and TTLs chosen as a consistency knob rather than inherited.

item.title: TLS is easy; rotating certificates without downtime is the real job
item.description: Certificates are time bombs with friendly names. Issue and renew them with a controller, make the rotation actually reach the pods, and terminate where your controls can read the request.

item.title: Load balancing — L4 moves connections, L7 makes decisions
item.description: "Load balancer" names two different machines: L4 spreads connections by tuple, L7 routes on the request. Most routing pain is asking L4 a question only L7 can answer.

item.title: SLOs and error budgets — turning "is it up?" into a number you can spend
item.description: An SLI measures what users feel, an SLO is the target, and the error budget is a currency: spend it on releases when there is budget, stop and harden when there is not.

item.title: Blue-green and canary — ship to a few before you ship to everyone
item.description: A deploy is a bet the new version works. Progressive delivery keeps most of the stake back — traffic-splitting plus a health signal, with rollback as the feature, not the fallback.

item.title: Defense in depth — no single wall, because walls fall
item.description: Security that needs one control to never fail is a countdown to a breach. Stack independent envelopes — identity, network, policy — so getting through one buys an attacker almost nothing.

item.title: Twelve-Factor isn't a checklist — it's what the platform makes free
item.description: The platform enforces most of the twelve so the app team gets them for free: config from a vault, stateless pods, logs as streams, disposability by default. Discipline becomes the shape of the paved road.

item.title: The OSI model, one layer at a time — and where each one runs here
item.description: Seven layers as a map of where a decision belongs: packet filtering at L3/4, load balancing at L4, routing and policy at L7, names resolved privately underneath. The layer tells you which repo to open.

item.title: You can't SSH into production — that's the feature
item.description: Every manual hot-fix is drift the code doesn't know about — and a box you can no longer rebuild. Immutable infrastructure removes the temptation by removing the door: change the code, roll a new one.

item.title: Replace, don't repair — cattle, not pets
item.description: Repairing a live instance is a bespoke, unrepeatable act that leaves you a slightly different system. Replacing it from code is boring, automatic and identical every time — which is why the platform does it for you.

item.title: Idempotency: declare the end state, run it twice
item.description: The quiet property that makes a platform safe to automate: Terraform applies to the same result, Argo CD syncs on a loop, a failed pipeline is just re-run. Without it every retry is a gamble.

item.title: CAP is a decision you already made — here's where
item.description: CAP isn't a whiteboard abstraction — you make the call every time you decide where data lives. Regional-by-default placement, per tenant-region secrets, and "global" reserved for what tolerates lag.

item.title: Well-architected is a set of questions, not a badge
item.description: The five pillars audited against a running platform — each answered with a mechanism you can click: reliability that rebuilds from code, three security envelopes, budgets with owners, a paved road, and capacity as a decision.

item.title: Migrating a self-managed GitLab to gitlab.com
item.description: Three independent migrations — users, repositories, artifacts — all asynchronous, so verify jobs, not calls. Plus the two coordination rules that save the cut-over: a freeze period and an immediate origin switch.

item.title: Terraform at scale — scopes, tiers & a policy gate
item.description: Why "one repo per concern, one scope per resource" beats a mono-state, and how an OPA gate makes apply boring.

item.title: Multi-tenant Kubernetes without the foot-guns
item.description: Namespaces as code, dedicated node pools, and why a tenant's data deliberately lives where the tenant can't delete it.

item.title: An AI layer for a developer platform
item.description: Grounding assistants in the platform's own knowledge graph and live state instead of hoping the model guesses right.

item.title: Your secrets don't live in your resource group
item.description: One Key Vault per tenant per region — deliberately placed in a platform-owned resource group, so a tenant can use its secrets but never destroy the vault.

item.title: A 403 is usually the fence doing its job
item.description: Tenants are isolated cells: near-admin inside, zero power outside, and no way to grant yourself in. A cross-tenant role-assignment 403 is that boundary made visible — not a missing permission.

item.title: A runner that can only touch its own tenant
item.description: GitLab is configured per tenant; the env vars pin each runner to a managed identity that can assign permissions only in its own tenant. The configuration is the security boundary — and the platform owns it.

item.title: A SAS token is a one-year password you forgot you minted
item.description: SAS tokens are long-lived, over-scoped bearer credentials you can't individually revoke — so clients never get one. A storage proxy authenticates with a managed identity, scopes each request, and can be cut off in one place.

item.title: Three libraries, one platform
item.description: Terraform modules, Helm charts and GitLab CI components — one reuse grammar (reference + version, never copy) with the OPA policy pack riding inside.

item.title: The golden path is three files, not a wiki page
item.description: A new service composes a pipeline component, Terraform modules and Helm charts — the paved road where doing it right is also the shortest route.

item.title: Instrumentation as a platform default — the OpenTelemetry Operator
item.description: A design note: collectors and auto-instrumentation as CRDs, so tenants inherit traces from their namespace instead of wiring SDKs by hand.

item.title: Nobody holds standing power
item.description: PIM-activated humans, standing operator identities for automation, membership as YAML merge requests, and secretless OIDC for CI.

item.title: Every alert email can prove where it came from
item.description: One shared email relay, one sender identity per tool — and a DKIM check inside every message that cryptographically proves its origin.

item.title: A cockpit for a fleet of agents
item.description: A which-key agent leader in tmux and agentsview — reading each session’s context fill from its transcript, so observing agents is free.

item.title: Attention is the bottleneck — signals from a working agent
item.description: Lifecycle hooks write per-session status files; the statusline spins while agents work and blinks when they need you — with GitLab events in the same strip.

item.title: Agent of Empires — sessions, worktrees, profiles, sandboxes
item.description: Each unit of work is a session with its own git worktree, an explicit identity profile, and — when trust is low — a sandbox. Tenancy ideas, applied to agents.

item.title: Run the pipeline before you push it
item.description: Local CI runs byte-identical to remote, a one-key diff that makes every divergence auditable, and a poller that watches the real pipeline after push.

item.title: Skills are golden paths for agents
item.description: Versioned, reviewable procedures the agent loads on demand — MR conventions, test-driven CI loops. The paved-road idea, applied to AI.

item.title: A statusline that knows who’s working — yas, wrapped
item.description: yet-another-statusline, untouched, plus a wrapper that splices in 📄 context files, 🧠 memory, the profile identity and a 🐳 sandbox badge.

item.title: fran-local-synapse — a marketplace for my agent’s habits
item.description: Personal skills organised as plugins in a local marketplace: working-on-ticket ceremonies, GitLab pipeline setup, CI watching, git guardrails.

item.title: Sandboxing Claude — three tools, three philosophies, and my setup
item.description: Docker sandboxes vs nono vs agent-cage — filesystem, permissions or egress — and my own: sandboxes + profile mounts + an Obsidian vault as the dynamic context bus.

item.title: What a secure agent sandbox should look like
item.description: I audited my agent runner’s sandbox and filed four upstream issues — least capability, least network, validated mounts, ephemeral credentials.

item.title: Gathering and filtering information — an agent reads my feeds
item.description: An RSS list fetched by an agent that scores every item against an interest profile written as a markdown note — and delivers a prioritized digest into my vault.

item.title: Grafana Cloud as the observability backend
item.description: Keep the opinionated half — collectors, tenancy labels, dashboards-as-code — and pay someone else to run Mimir at 3 a.m. Tenancy labels ARE the cost model.

item.title: Migrating observability: on-premises → Grafana Cloud
item.description: Dual-write at the agents, migrate the readers, starve the old stack — and the three things that actually bit: cardinality, retention, auth.

item.title: From on-premises to cloud — migrate the operating model
item.description: Guardrails first, workloads through the golden path, and an old environment that gets starved rather than switched off.

item.title: Moving a platform between Azure subscriptions
item.description: Same cloud, same code, different boundary: recreate the scope, repoint state/identity/DNS/peering, dual-run until the diff is only intentional.

item.title: The landscape — CNCF & friends I actually run
item.description: Not a logo wall: every tool runs in the platform today, earns its place, and is GitOps-delivered by cluster class — base everywhere, hub extras once, dev tooling never in live.

item.title: cert-manager — certificates as a controller, not a calendar entry
item.description: CSR → issue → store → renew before expiry, reconciled by a controller instead of a human — installed first among cluster services because everything with a hostname depends on it.

item.title: Argo CD — the cluster state is a repo
item.description: App-of-apps per cluster, drift as a dashboard state, no kubectl in pipelines — and Argo manages Argo, so terraform only seeds the first install.

item.title: Kyverno — safe namespaces by default
item.description: Validate, mutate, generate — the runtime half of the policy gate, sync-waved at −2 so admission policy exists before the first tenant namespace ever syncs.

item.title: External Secrets — Key Vault to pods, no humans
item.description: Key Vault → Kubernetes secrets without a person in the loop; workloads reference ExternalSecret outputs on their very first sync.

item.title: Reloader — rotation that actually reaches pods
item.description: A rotated secret restarts the pods that mount it — closing the last mile of External Secrets so rotation is real, not cosmetic.

item.title: External DNS — records follow the routes
item.description: Watches the HTTPRoutes tenants create and reconciles the platform DNS zone — nobody files a ticket for a CNAME.

item.title: KEDA — scale on real signals
item.description: Queues and events instead of CPU guesses, including scale-to-zero — event-driven autoscaling every tenant inherits.

item.title: Karpenter — just-in-time, right-sized nodes
item.description: Provisioned in seconds, consolidated when idle: system pools stay terraform-owned, burst capacity is Karpenter-owned.

item.title: OpenTelemetry — instrument once, everywhere
item.description: One collector per cluster (daemonset + gateway): tenants instrument once against OTLP and the platform decides where telemetry lands.

item.title: Grafana — one pane, run once
item.description: Dashboards, alerts and Explore as code over Mimir & Loki — hub-only by design: regional clusters ship telemetry, they don't each run a dashboard stack.

item.title: Telepresence — debug the real cluster, safely
item.description: Intercept a Service from the laptop — a sandbox-cluster feature by placement, because the same trick in live is an incident.

item.title: Backstage — the developer portal
item.description: Software catalog, golden-path scaffolder and TechDocs — hub-only: one catalog, one scaffolder, backed by the postgresql-k8s module.

item.title: Cloud Native Buildpacks — images without Dockerfiles
item.description: kpack turns source into an OCI image on the hardened base without a hand-written Dockerfile — one builder to patch, not one Dockerfile per repo.

item.title: Trivy — continuous vulnerability scanning, not just a build-time gate
item.description: Scans every running workload on a schedule — so a CVE disclosed the day after a deploy is caught, not just the one that existed at build time.

item.title: Policy Reporter — one dashboard for every policy engine
item.description: Reads the PolicyReport CRDs Kyverno and Trivy already emit and turns them into one UI plus Slack/Teams alerts — a standard, not a custom exporter.

item.title: OpenCost — cost allocation, per tenant, per namespace
item.description: Cost per namespace and workload from real requests/usage against actual pricing — the number behind "~90% cost cut," visible to anyone on the platform.

item.title: OPA / rego — infrastructure can't change unless policy says it may
item.description: A plan → OPA evaluation → apply safety gate, composable per cloud provider — the safe choice (paranoid/high/standard) is the default, not an opt-in.

item.title: Falco — the third layer: catching what already got past the first two
item.description: eBPF syscall watching for what admission policy and image scans can't see — a shell spawned inside a container, a write to /etc/shadow, an unexpected connection.

item.title: Litmus — chaos as a reviewed experiment, never a surprise
item.description: Controlled failure to prove resilience claims instead of hoping them — every experiment is a reviewed ChaosEngine CRD, scoped to one namespace, opt-in only.

item.title: OpenFeature — decouple the deploy from the release
item.description: A vendor-neutral feature-flag spec + SDK backed by flagd in-cluster — dark-launch a feature before it's a canary rollout, not after.

item.title: Cilium — the CNI, chosen at cluster creation, not GitOps'd in later
item.description: Azure CNI powered by Cilium: eBPF dataplane set at cluster creation, not a Helm chart installed after — L3-L7 network policy and Hubble visibility in one dataplane's job.

item.title: Dapr — building-block APIs a sidecar gives every language
item.description: Pub/sub, state, service invocation and durable workflow over one sidecar API — the durable-workflow primitive agentic AI pipelines need without hand-rolling it.

item.title: Traefik — one shared gateway, many tenant routes
item.description: Exactly ONE gateway instance per cluster, platform-owned; tenants attach namespace-scoped HTTPRoutes by parentRef and never run their own ingress — SSO rides as an oauth2-proxy sidecar, so the gateway stays auth-agnostic.

item.title: Helm — the packaging grammar
item.description: One chart library consumed everywhere — and deliberately NO controller in the cluster: charts are OCI artifacts Argo CD renders server-side.
